pack.name: Everyday expression pack
pack.description: Three practical words for testing WordFlow's full word-detail experience.

items.meaning: Fluent, persuasive, and graceful in speaking or writing.
items.explanation: Use it to praise someone who expresses ideas clearly and beautifully, especially in a speech or piece of writing.
items.origin: From Latin eloquens, meaning speaking out or fluent, from eloqui: to speak out.
examples: Her eloquent speech moved the entire audience.
He wrote an eloquent letter of thanks.
The lawyer gave an eloquent closing argument.
She is eloquent when explaining difficult ideas.
His silence was more eloquent than a long reply.

items.meaning: Dealing with problems in a practical and realistic way.
items.explanation: Use it for a person, decision, or plan focused on what will work in real life rather than on ideal theories.
items.origin: From Greek pragmatikos, meaning relating to action or business, from pragma: a deed or matter.
examples: We need a pragmatic solution to the budget problem.
She took a pragmatic approach to finding a new job.
His pragmatic advice helped the team move forward.
The plan is ambitious but still pragmatic.
Being pragmatic does not mean giving up on your goals.

items.meaning: Able to recover quickly after difficulty, stress, or change.
items.explanation: Use it to describe people, communities, or systems that adapt and recover after setbacks.
items.origin: From Latin resilire, meaning to spring back or rebound.
examples: Children can be remarkably resilient after a major change.
The resilient team recovered quickly from the failed launch.
She remained resilient during a difficult year.
A resilient system can keep working during an outage.
Building resilient habits takes time and patience.
